philosophy.title: Why we claim stars
philosophy.lede: Star.org is not just a commemorative keepsake shop. Behind it lies a whole set of ideas about how a civilization measures itself, how the universe gets developed, and how each person takes part — written up as five ideas and a whitepaper.
philosophy.i1Title: A civilization is measured by information utilization
philosophy.i1Body: We habitually measure civilization by energy utilization: how much energy you can harness decides which rung you stand on. We propose another, equally fundamental yardstick — information utilization, the degree to which a civilization grasps true information about the universe. By this measure Earth has not yet reached Information Civilization, Level One (team estimate: about 0.7) — the threshold is all of humanity in an ongoing relationship with at least one star.
philosophy.i2Title: The universe has three ores; we mine the information ore
philosophy.i2Body: The universe holds three fundamentally different resources: information ore, energy ore, and matter ore. Energy ore and matter ore both require enormous industrial and spacefaring capacity to touch. Only information ore asks not for a starship but for attention — the one resource every person can start on immediately. So that is what we develop.
philosophy.i3Title: The key to a bond with a star is the right to name
philosophy.i3Body: The biggest bottleneck in developing space is that it makes ordinary people feel it has nothing to do with them. To involve all of humanity, each person first needs a real bond with the sky — the right to name. Name and claim a real star, and it stops being a point of light on a backdrop and becomes “my star.” (This is a personal bond of emotion and memory, not official IAU naming.)
philosophy.i4Title: Whoever pays attention is developing it
philosophy.i4Body: To “develop” information ore is not to dig it open but to observe, record, understand, and tell it. So whoever observes or attends to a star's information is developing that star's information ore, and therefore holds a certain information right over it. We make that record public, transparent and independently verifiable.
philosophy.i5Title: Not in body — but in information and imagination
philosophy.i5Body: Our bodies cannot reach the distant stars, but our information and imagination can. The Three-Body Problem, Star Trek, and the starfields of every game turn human attention and imagination toward the cosmos — a special mode of mining information ore that completes the mining of real celestial data.
philosophy.readNote: The full argument lives on the philosophy page — all five ideas, the comparison table of the three ores, and the TeX-typeset whitepaper.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is this official naming by the International Astronomical Union (IAU)?
faq.a1: No. Scientific naming of stars is administered by the International Astronomical Union, and we cannot and do not claim to provide official naming. What this service offers is a commemorative, publicly verifiable claim: the star itself is real, and the coordinates, magnitude, spectral type and distance on the certificate come from public astronomical catalogues — but this claim confers no naming right over any celestial body, and will not be used by the astronomical community as an official name. Please confirm before ordering that this matches what you expect.
faq.q2: Could my star be claimed by someone else too?
faq.a2: No. Each star in the pool is allocated exactly once, is written to the public registry the moment it is allocated, and the allocation runs serially so two orders arriving at the same instant cannot take the same star. Anyone can search the star identifier in the public registry and confirm there is only one record. If a duplicate ever occurs through our mistake, we refund it unconditionally or reprocess it.
faq.q3: What can I do with the claim afterwards?
faq.a3: You can download the PDF certificate (printable, displayable), share the permanent link on social platforms (optimised for the X share card), or simply keep it as a record belonging to the two of you. As long as this service is running the link stays valid, and it does not depend on you keeping the email; the record is stored as plain text in a public repository, so you can keep your own copy.
faq.a4: This service delivers an instantly generated digital keepsake, so we do not offer refunds for reasons other than quality — please confirm this before buying. If the problem is on our side — a duplicate allocation, an incorrect certificate, or a payment that produced no certificate — we will contact you within 24 hours and refund unconditionally or reprocess it.
faq.q5: How soon after payment do I get the certificate?
faq.a5: Usually within 1–3 minutes, and never more than 5. The checkout completion page also states that the certificate will be sent to your email address. If you have not received it within 24 hours, write to {{supportEmail}} with the email address you used at checkout and we will resend it manually.
faq.q6: Will my personal information be made public?
faq.a6: The public registry contains only the star identifier, the display name, the dedication (if any) and the claim date. Email addresses and order details are never written to any public file. You can choose anonymous display at checkout, in which case not even the display name appears on the public page or in the registry.
faq.q7: Why can't I pick my own star?
faq.a7: The system randomly assigns one unclaimed star from the pool, so everyone has the same chance and nobody can know in advance which star they will get. Every claim therefore corresponds to a real, naked-eye star (fainter ones are easier to see away from light pollution), and it removes the hesitation and waiting that a "pick your star" step would introduce.
faq.q8: By information utilization, what level is Earth at?
faq.a8: Not yet at Level One — the team estimate is about 0.7. The criterion is not that we know little, but that our information reach and our action reach are wildly out of balance: we receive light from 13.8 billion years ago, and the observable universe has a comoving radius of about 46 billion light-years — while Voyager 1, the farthest object we have ever sent, is about 172 AU (roughly 0.0027 light-years), only about 0.06% of the way to the nearest star (Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years). That is some 13 orders of magnitude apart. Seeing without being able to act is what Level One means; a civilization reaches Level Two when observation and action close the loop.
faq.q9: What do you mean by “information ore”?
faq.a9: The universe holds three fundamentally different resources: energy ore (energy that can be harnessed), matter ore (physical substance that can be collected or manufactured), and information ore (information about celestial bodies and phenomena: position, magnitude, distance, spectrum, motion, history). The first two require enormous industrial and spacefaring capacity before they can be touched at all. Only information ore asks not for a starship but for attention — the one of the three that anyone can start on immediately.
faq.q10: Does claiming a star count as developing it?
faq.a10: Yes. For information ore, to develop is not to dig it open but to observe, record, understand and tell it. Naming a real star and then attending to it over time is how that star's information ore gets mined — which is why we treat the right to name as the key between a person and the sky. To be clear, the name here is a personal memorial and observation marker set up for you; it does not constitute, and does not claim to be, official naming by the International Astronomical Union (IAU).
faq.a11: Yes. The full argument for all five ideas is on the philosophy page, which also offers the TeX-typeset philosophy whitepaper (English and Chinese editions, A4) that opens directly in your browser.

philosophy.title: The height of a civilization is also decided by how much of the universe it can see clearly
philosophy.lede: Humanity already measures the height of a civilization by its energy. We want to establish how much of the universe we understand as a measure in its own right. The five ideas below are not parallel slogans but a single chain of reasoning that joins end to end: from the yardstick, to the resource, to the participants, to the rights, and finally to another way of reaching the cosmos.
philosophy.whitepaperLede: The full argument — all five ideas, the comparison table of the three ores, and the summary chain — has been typeset into a whitepaper with TeX. We suggest reading the whitepaper first, then coming back to this web summary.
philosophy.whitepaperNote: Both editions have identical content, are A4, and are ready to print.
philosophy.s1Title: 1. Civilization level: from energy utilization to information utilization
philosophy.s1Body: The most commonly cited yardstick for civilization is energy utilization: how much energy a civilization can harness determines its place on the cosmic ladder. From burning wood and coal, to nuclear fission, to the hypothetical Dyson sphere that wraps a star, the scale is a magnitude of energy. This yardstick carries a hidden premise — it measures what a civilization can do, not what it knows. Star.org proposes another, equally fundamental yardstick: information utilization, the degree to which a civilization grasps true information about the universe and can turn it into understanding and action. It measures a civilization's cognitive frontier, not its power ceiling. The two are not opposed: energy decides whether a civilization can move, information decides whether it can see.
philosophy.s1Note: By information utilization, Earth has not yet reached “Information Civilization, Level One” (team estimate about 0.7): the threshold is complete participation on the observation side — all of humanity in an ongoing relationship with at least one celestial body. We have only just begun to systematically record and share the universe's information planet-wide, and the celestial bodies we can see, measure and describe are an extremely small patch relative to the whole cosmos. This is the starting point, not the endpoint.
philosophy.s2Title: 2. Three kinds of ore in the universe: information, energy, matter
philosophy.s2Body: If we treat the universe as a treasure to be developed, it consists of three fundamentally different resources. Energy ore is the energy that can be harnessed, and demands engineering and industrial capacity. Matter ore is physical substance that can be collected or manufactured, and demands the ability to reach and extract. Information ore is information about celestial bodies and phenomena — position, magnitude, distance, spectrum, motion, history, even the stories behind them — and demands not a starship but attention. The difference among the three is not how precious they are but the barrier to entry: energy and matter ore are out of reach for an individual, while information ore is open to everyone.
philosophy.s2Note: Star.org focuses on developing information ore, because among the three it is the only resource that lets all of humanity get started immediately, without first colonizing the cosmos.
philosophy.s3Title: 3. How to mobilize all of humanity: a bond with the stars, and the right to name
philosophy.s3Body: The grand narrative of humanity developing the cosmos tends to make ordinary people feel that it is a matter for astronauts, scientists and billionaires. When something has no concrete connection to an individual, it generates no real drive to participate. Among all the ways of forging a bond, we hold that the most fundamental and most moving is the right to name: to name a star is humanity's oldest and most instinctive act of cognition, and once a name is given, that star stops being a point of light on a backdrop and becomes “my star” — a concrete, identifiable, callable sense of belonging.
philosophy.s3Note: An important clarification: “naming / claiming” here is a personal bond of emotion and cognition — an observation and memorial marker that a namer establishes for a real celestial body. It does not constitute, and does not claim to be, a naming right granted by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) or any other official body.
philosophy.s4Title: 4. Information rights: whoever attends, develops — and therefore holds
philosophy.s4Body: For a star's information ore, to “develop” is not to dig it open but to observe, record, understand and tell it. Three steps follow. Attention = development: every act of attention is an act of extraction from that star's information ore. Development = contribution: the attention, observation, stories and memory a person invests are real and indelible. Investment = right: whoever pays attention to a star holds a certain right over its information — one that can be marked, recorded and preserved long-term.
philosophy.s4Note: This right is an identifiable, recordable and preservable bond of attention; a record of developing that star's information ore; and a memorial and emotional belonging that belongs to the namer. It is not physical possession of the star itself, not exclusive control of all astronomical data about it (the real data belongs to the scientific commons and to all humanity), and not a transferable financial instrument whose value can grow. The site does not treat a star as property to be handed over, does not turn it into a financial product, and does not present it as something that will gain in value.
philosophy.s5Title: 5. Not in body — but in information and imagination
philosophy.s5Body: Physically, the human body is confined to Earth; for any foreseeable future, energy ore and matter ore are beyond the reach of the vast majority of people. But what defines a person or a civilization is not only where its body resides, but how far its information has reached and how far its imagination extends. The science fiction of The Three-Body Problem, the film and television of Star Trek, and the starfields of games all turn human attention and imagination toward the cosmos. They extract not a gram of matter and not a wisp of energy, yet they mine the most precious thing of all: humanity's understanding and imagination of who we are and where in the universe we stand.
philosophy.s5Note: Imagination needs real celestial information as its soil, and real information needs imagination to give it meaning. Claiming a real star is mining that star's information ore; being stirred toward the sky by science fiction and games is also mining humanity's collective information ore — different veins of the same ore.
